name: West Sumatra
summary_text: The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people recorded as swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance). Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft (ranperda, articles 13-14) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah plus mandated "rehabilitation" (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other provinces (not West Sumatra itself, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this province's bylaws instantiate. This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning (an Aceh-specific penalty) or prosecution under these provisions is recorded. It remains above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.

sources.title: Penerapan Perda Bukittinggi Nomor 2 Tahun 2024 tentang Ketertiban Umum terhadap LGBT Studi Kasus Kota Bukittinggi Ditinjau dari Fiqih Siyasah Tanfidziyah | AHKAM
sources.claim_summary: 2026 empirical-legal field study (Ahkam journal) of the implementation of Bukittinggi Perda No. 2 of 2024 against LGBT people: enforcement runs through supervision, raids and guidance by Satpol PP with customary (LKAAM), religious (MUI) and Bundo Kanduang institutions; implementation obstacles include leaked raid information, suboptimal sanctions, weak rehabilitation capacity and low public awareness.

2025 study (Al-Dyas) of non-state-actor handling of LGBT cases in Bukittinggi: recorded cases rose from 56 people in 2023 to 272 in 2024 (figures from app detections and razias); the Kurai customary-law community initiated the customary sanction dibuang sepanjang adat, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance, and a barcode registration system for boarding houses; customary sanctions depend on police follow-through.

sources.title: DPRD Limapuluh Kota Finalisasi Ranperda Anti-LGBT, Memuat Denda Administratif dan Rehabilitasi - Mimbarsumbar.id
sources.claim_summary: March 2026 report: the Limapuluh Kota regional legislature finalised an anti-LGBT draft bylaw (Ranperda on public order, articles 13-14) containing an explicit prohibition of same-sex behaviour, administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah, and mandated rehabilitation (psychosocial diagnosis and counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) with local-government clinics; the council acknowledges expected pro-contra backlash.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta) - the reference for Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism; West Sumatra's newer Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping.
